lessonTitle: Teratogens and Critical Periods: Drugs, Infections, Toxins and Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder

blocks.text: The same exposure can do nothing, cause a malformed heart, or damage the fetal kidneys, depending only on the week of pregnancy in which it occurs. A pharmacist asked whether a medicine is safe in pregnancy always has to ask first: how many weeks along is she?

blocks.title: Teratogen
blocks.text: A teratogen is any agent (a drug, infection, chemical, physical agent or maternal condition) that, when present during development, causes a structural or functional abnormality in the embryo or fetus, or growth restriction or death. About 3% of babies are born with a major congenital anomaly, and only a minority of anomalies are attributable to a recognised teratogen.

blocks.markdown: **General principles of teratology.** (1) **Timing** of exposure is critical: the effect depends on the developmental stage. (2) **Dose and duration**: higher or more prolonged exposure usually produces more severe effects, and there may be a threshold. (3) **Genotype** of mother and fetus (for example in drug metabolism and placental transfer) influences susceptibility. (4) Each agent acts through a **specific mechanism** and produces a characteristic pattern of defects. (5) The manifestations may be **death, malformation, growth restriction or functional (especially neurobehavioural) deficit**. (6) Access to the fetus depends on the agent's ability to cross the placenta; many drugs of small molecular size cross freely.

**Critical periods.** Counting from fertilisation: during the **first two weeks** (before and during implantation, the 'all-or-none' period) a damaging exposure usually kills the embryo or is repaired by the many totipotent cells, so the pregnancy either miscarries or continues normally. The **embryonic period (weeks 3-8)** is the time of organogenesis and the period of **maximal susceptibility to structural malformation**, and each organ has its own critical window (neural tube closes by the end of week 4; the heart is sensitive during weeks 3-8; limbs during weeks 4-8; the palate to about week 12). In the **fetal period (week 9 to birth)** the organs are formed, so teratogens more often cause growth restriction, reduced organ function or damage to the central nervous system, which continues to develop throughout pregnancy and after birth.

headers: Typical effect of a teratogenic exposure
rows: Death of the embryo or no effect (all or none)
Growth restriction, functional and CNS damage, minor anomalies
Alcohol; ACE inhibitors causing fetal kidney failure; tobacco causing growth restriction
blocks.caption: Timing of exposure determines the kind of defect.

blocks.title: Dating an exposure to a critical period
blocks.prompt: A woman with a regular 28-day cycle took a known teratogenic drug for one week, starting 6 weeks after her last menstrual period. Which developmental period did this correspond to, and what kind of defect would you worry about?

steps.text: Convert gestational age (from the last menstrual period) to embryonic age by subtracting about 2 weeks: 6 - 2 = 4 weeks after fertilisation.
A week starting at embryonic week 4 and ending at week 5 lies within the embryonic period (weeks 3-8), during organogenesis.
This is the time of maximal susceptibility to major structural malformations (heart, limbs, neural tube closing at the end of week 4, eyes and ears), rather than a mainly growth or functional effect.

blocks.answer: Embryonic weeks 4-5, the organogenesis period of highest risk for major structural malformations.

blocks.markdown: **Examples of teratogens.** Drugs (pharmacology teaching examples; no dosing advice is intended): **valproate** (neural tube defects, craniofacial anomalies, and neurodevelopmental impairment); **warfarin** (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses and CNS defects in early pregnancy); **isotretinoin**, a retinoid (craniofacial, cardiac, thymic and CNS malformations); **ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers** in the second and third trimesters (fetal renal failure with oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia); **tetracyclines** (staining of developing teeth and bone effects); **methotrexate** and **misoprostol**; **thalidomide** (limb reduction defects). **Infections** are often remembered as the TORCH group: **T**oxoplasmosis (hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis), **R**ubella (patent ductus arteriosus or pulmonary artery stenosis, cataracts, sensorineural deafness), **C**ytomegalovirus (microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, hearing loss), **H**erpes simplex, and **O**thers (syphilis, varicella, Zika virus with microcephaly, parvovirus B19). **Toxins and other factors:** alcohol, tobacco (growth restriction), cocaine, lead, methylmercury, ionising radiation, and poorly controlled maternal diabetes mellitus (neural tube, cardiac and caudal anomalies, macrosomia).

rows: Neural tube defects, facial dysmorphism, neurodevelopmental impairment
Nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, CNS defects
Cardiac and neural tube defects, macrosomia
blocks.caption: Selected human teratogens.

blocks.title: Linking a finding to the likely agent
blocks.prompt: A newborn has cataracts, sensorineural deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus. The mother had a mild rash with fever in the first trimester. Identify the likely agent and explain why timing matters.

steps.text: The triad of cataracts, deafness and a cardiac lesion (PDA) with a first-trimester rash points to congenital rubella syndrome.
Infection during weeks 3-8, when the heart, eye lens and inner ear are forming, causes major structural damage; infection later in pregnancy more often causes growth restriction or milder defects.
Prevention is by maternal immunisation before pregnancy, because live vaccines are not given during pregnancy.

blocks.answer: Congenital rubella; the timing of infection during organogenesis explains the structural defects.

blocks.title: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD)
blocks.text: FASD is the range of physical, brain and behavioural abnormalities caused by prenatal alcohol exposure; fetal alcohol syndrome is the most severe, recognisable end. Ethanol crosses the placenta freely, and no safe level of alcohol in pregnancy has been established.

blocks.markdown: **Features of FASD.** The classical features of fetal alcohol syndrome fall into three groups: (1) a characteristic **facial appearance**: short palpebral fissures, a smooth (flattened) philtrum and a thin upper lip (vermilion border); (2) **growth deficiency**, both prenatal and postnatal (small for gestational age, short stature, low weight); (3) **central nervous system abnormality**: microcephaly, intellectual disability, learning and attention problems, hyperactivity, poor social and executive function. Other associated findings include congenital heart defects (such as ventricular septal defects), skeletal and renal anomalies. The brain is affected throughout pregnancy, so neurodevelopmental effects occur with exposure at any stage, whereas the facial features relate to exposure in the early weeks. Many affected children have no distinctive facial features, which is why 'spectrum' is used.

items: Timing: all-or-none (weeks 1-2), major malformations (weeks 3-8), growth and CNS effects (week 9 onward).
Drugs: valproate, warfarin, isotretinoin, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines; infections: TORCH.
FASD: smooth philtrum, short palpebral fissures, thin upper lip, growth restriction, CNS impairment.
Most teratogenic harm is preventable by pre-pregnancy counselling and medication review.

blocks.title: A drug can be harmful at one time and safe at another
blocks.text: Risk depends on timing and dose. Women should never stop a necessary medicine without advice; instead, medication should be reviewed before conception or as soon as pregnancy is suspected.

points: A teratogen causes structural or functional defects, growth restriction or death; the effect depends on timing, dose, genotype and the agent's mechanism.
Weeks 3-8 (organogenesis) are the time of greatest risk for major malformations; later exposure tends to cause growth or functional damage; exposure in weeks 1-2 is all or none.
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder comprises a characteristic face (short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip), growth restriction and CNS dysfunction.

questions.stem: Which period of development is most susceptible to the induction of major structural malformations by a teratogen?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the period of organogenesis.
distractorRationale.b: The first two weeks are the all-or-none period.
distractorRationale.c: Third-trimester exposures more often affect growth and function.
distractorRationale.d: Perinatal exposures act on an already formed infant.

questions.explanation: Organs form in weeks 3-8 so a teratogen acting then can disturb the formation of structures. Before this, damage tends to kill the embryo or be compensated; after this, organs are formed and effects are mainly on growth and function.

questions.stem: A woman who took an ACE inhibitor throughout the second and third trimesters delivers an infant with anuria, hypoplastic lungs and limb contractures after oligohydramnios. Why is this effect seen with exposure at this stage, rather than a major structural anomaly of the heart?

options.text: The heart was already formed; late exposure impairs fetal renal perfusion and function instead
ACE inhibitors cannot cross the placenta in the first trimester
The fetal kidney is not formed until after birth
All teratogens act only in the third trimester

questions.correctOptionText: The heart was already formed; late exposure impairs fetal renal perfusion and function instead

distractorRationale.a: Correct: organogenesis was complete, and the fetal kidney depends on the renin-angiotensin system for perfusion.
distractorRationale.b: ACE inhibitors cross the placenta throughout pregnancy.
distractorRationale.c: Fetal kidneys produce urine from the late first trimester onwards.
distractorRationale.d: Teratogens act at various stages depending on the agent.

questions.explanation: Late in pregnancy the organs are already formed, so the main effect is functional: ACE inhibitors reduce fetal renal perfusion, causing renal failure and oligohydramnios, which leads to pulmonary hypoplasia and contractures.

questions.stem: A mother who had a flu-like illness with a rash in early pregnancy gives birth to an infant with cataracts, sensorineural hearing loss and a persistent patent ductus arteriosus. Which infection is the most likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cataracts, deafness and PDA are the classical triad of congenital rubella.
distractorRationale.b: Toxoplasmosis gives chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcification.
distractorRationale.c: CMV gives microcephaly, periventricular calcification and hearing loss but cataract and PDA are not the classical combination.
distractorRationale.d: Parvovirus mainly causes fetal anaemia and hydrops.

questions.explanation: Cataracts, sensorineural deafness and a cardiac lesion such as PDA is the classical triad of congenital rubella syndrome, typical when infection occurs in the first trimester. The other infections have different characteristic patterns.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum, a thin upper lip, a head circumference below the 3rd centile, poor attention and learning difficulties. Growth has been below the 3rd centile since birth. Which prenatal exposure is the most likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the pattern of fetal alcohol syndrome.
distractorRationale.b: Warfarin produces nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses.
distractorRationale.c: Rubella produces cataracts, deafness and heart defects.

questions.explanation: The triad of characteristic facial features (short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip), growth deficiency and CNS dysfunction defines fetal alcohol syndrome, the severe end of FASD.

questions.stem: In a registry, major malformations occurred in 12 of 100 pregnancies exposed to a drug in the first trimester and in 3 of 100 unexposed pregnancies. What is the relative risk of malformation with exposure? Give a ratio.
questions.explanation: Relative risk is the risk in the exposed group divided by the risk in the unexposed group: 0.12 / 0.03 = 4. The absolute increase is 9 percentage points, which is also important when counselling.

questions.stem: A woman with a regular 28-day cycle is 10 weeks from her last menstrual period when a teratogenic exposure is identified, having occurred 11 days ago. What was the embryonic age (in weeks after fertilisation) at the time of exposure, to one decimal place? Take fertilisation to occur 14 days after the LMP.
questions.explanation: She is now 10 weeks = 70 days from the LMP; the exposure was 11 days earlier, at day 59 from the LMP. Fertilisation occurred at day 14, so the embryonic age at exposure was 59 - 14 = 45 days, which is 45/7 = 6.4 weeks. This lies in the organogenesis period (weeks 3-8).

questions.stem: True or false: A teratogenic exposure in the first two weeks after fertilisation most often results in either miscarriage or a normal pregnancy rather than a specific malformation.
questions.explanation: In the first two weeks, damage to a few cells either kills the embryo or is compensated by the remaining totipotent cells, which is the all-or-none principle. Specific malformations are mainly produced during organogenesis.

questions.stem: Define a teratogen and explain, using examples, why the timing of exposure determines the type of defect.
markingGuide: Teratogen: an agent that causes structural or functional abnormality, growth restriction or death in the embryo or fetus.
Weeks 1-2: all-or-none effect (death or normal development).
Weeks 3-8: organogenesis, with each organ having its own critical window, so major malformations arise (e.g. neural tube defects with valproate, craniofacial and cardiac defects with isotretinoin).
Week 9 to term: organs formed; effects on growth, function and CNS (e.g. alcohol, ACE inhibitors causing renal failure).
Other determinants: dose, genotype, specific mechanism, placental transfer.
questions.explanation: Each tissue is vulnerable only while it is forming, so the same agent causes different defects at different times.

questions.stem: Give two drugs, two infections and two other toxins or maternal conditions that are known to be teratogenic, and state one characteristic effect of each.
markingGuide: Two drugs with effects, e.g. valproate (neural tube defect, neurodevelopmental impairment), warfarin (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses), isotretinoin (craniofacial and cardiac defects), ACE inhibitors (fetal renal failure).
Two infections with effects, e.g. rubella (cataracts, deafness, PDA), CMV (microcephaly, hearing loss), toxoplasmosis (hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis), Zika (microcephaly).
Two other agents, e.g. alcohol (FASD), tobacco (growth restriction), lead, methylmercury, radiation, poorly controlled maternal diabetes (cardiac and neural tube defects).
questions.explanation: Marks are awarded for correct agent-effect pairs, which show knowledge of the patterns of teratogenic damage.

questions.stem: Describe the clinical features of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder in three categories, and explain why not all affected children have the typical facial features.
markingGuide: Facial features: short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip.
Growth: prenatal and postnatal growth deficiency.
CNS: microcephaly, intellectual disability, learning, attention and behavioural problems.
Associated anomalies: cardiac (e.g. VSD), skeletal, renal.
Spectrum: facial features reflect exposure at a critical early window and dose, whereas the brain is vulnerable throughout pregnancy; many children have CNS problems without the classical face.
No safe level of alcohol is established.
questions.explanation: FASD is a spectrum: fetal alcohol syndrome is the full picture, but neurodevelopmental effects occur with or without the typical face because of timing and dose.
